Background The technology of oral fluid testing for misused drugs is at an advanced stage ( ; ; ; ;; ; ; ; ; ; ), but urine remains the standard matrix for drug screening in most community settings, including addiction treatment ( ; ); community corrections ( ), screening in primary care ( ; ), drug courts ( ), child protective services (Child Trends, 2017), workplace safety monitoring ( ; ), offender monitoring ( ; ), sports doping surveillance ( ; ) and other outpatient and field settings. However, oral fluid testing has several known advantages over urine analysis, specifically the elimination of privacy issues, the need to provide urine on demand, the need for restroom access, the possible need for a same-gender observer, the near-elimination of potential dilution or adulteration of specimens ( ; ; ) and the greater willingness in voluntary studies to provide oral fluid instead of urine ( ) or instead of hair ( ). Also note that primary care physicians say that urine testing for misused drugs is generally difficult to implement ( ). Oral fluid testing has been approved for clinical use by the ; ) and is included in testing recommendations by the . Although the window of detection for oral fluid has been a concern since its introduction ( ; ), more recent research based on state of the art techniques for both urine analysis and oral fluid analysis, including some controlled administration studies, indicates that the window of detection for these matrices is similar for several major drugs ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ), although relative detection windows for cocaine metabolites remain unclear ( ; ; ). Indirect evidence also suggests similar windows of detection for oral fluid and urine, in that workplace-testing programs nationally usually yield the same or higher drug positive rates for oral fluid than for urine over the last two decades ( ; ); the sometimes lower rates for urine are probably due to adulterated or diluted specimens in unobserved settings rather than the test technology. National U.S. epidemiological studies, where biomarkers from urine, blood or hair are difficult or impossible to obtain, continue to rely on self-reports of drug use, e.g., the National Household Survey ( ) and Monitoring the Future ( ), despite standing evidence that biomarkers detect considerably more drug use than self-reports (e.g., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). This is especially important because timely drug surveillance is critical for early detection and tracking of local and national drug epidemics, such as the current U.S. opiate and specifically fentanyl crises ( ; ). An important barrier to the wider use of oral fluid for testing for misused drugs is the small number of studies employing state-of-the-art testing that directly compare the results for oral fluid with urine, the most widely accepted and used matrix, for paired specimens provided by the same individuals at the same time. The most frequent type of previous study, although still few in number, compares liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS) results (a definitive test) between urine and oral fluid. Almost all of these studies have had one or more significant limitations: small subject sample sizes; limited types or numbers of drugs studied, either purposely or de facto; very low prevalence rates for many drugs; and sometimes, different testing protocols for oral fluid and urine within the same study ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). The only large sample study was . Generally, there are numerous inconsistencies in this literature, so that another broad-based, large sample study, such as the current research, is useful to conduct. It is important to note that physiological and biochemical factors may alter drug disposition in oral fluid as compared with urine, which must be considered when interpreting differences in results ( ). One finding is that parent drugs are often more detectable in oral fluid whereas their metabolites tend to be more detectable in urine ( ; ; ). One review identifies the mechanism as “renal excretion favoring water-soluble metabolite elimination, whereas oral fluid excretion favoring parent drugs capable of rapid passive diffusion across membranes” ( ). As another example, chemical properties such as acidity and glucuronidation appear to explain differences in detection rates of individual opioids and benzodiazepines in oral fluid vs. urine ( ; ). The clinical relevance of current studies comparing oral fluid with urine is limited, because none included presumptive tests (e.g., screening by immunoassay) which, followed by confirmation of positives by a definitive test, is the current standard for clinical drug monitoring. This protocol continues to be widely used despite clear clinical benefits of direct-to-definitive testing ( ; ; ; ). Although there is a body of research on the accuracy of presumptive tests in urine

properties such as acidity and glucuronidation appear to explain differences in detection rates of individual opioids and benzodiazepines in oral fluid vs. urine ( ; ). The clinical relevance of current studies comparing oral fluid with urine is limited, because none included presumptive tests (e.g., screening by immunoassay) which, followed by confirmation of positives by a definitive test, is the current standard for clinical drug monitoring. This protocol continues to be widely used despite clear clinical benefits of direct-to-definitive testing ( ; ; ; ). Although there is a body of research on the accuracy of presumptive tests in urine (e.g., ; ; ; ), there is little similar research on the accuracy of presumptive tests in oral fluid that were conducted in field settings, with two early exceptions being and . Moreover, even the research on urine is almost always focused on detection of false screening positives ( ), rather than the arguably equally important detection of false screening negatives ( ; ). Wider use of oral fluid for clinical drug monitoring would be justified if the accuracy of presumptive plus confirmation testing and/or direct-to-definitive testing were shown to be similar for urine and oral fluid, “accuracy” being defined as the minimization of both false positive and false negatives ( ). 1.1 Study Objectives. Compare the results of presumptive immunoassay screens plus LC-MS-MS confirmation of positives vs. direct-to-definitive LC-MS/MS testing for major drug classes in oral fluid and urine. Compare the results of oral fluid vs. urine for identifying specific misused drugs by direct-to-definitive LC-MS-MS testing. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1 Participants and setting The participants were individuals applying for methadone treatment in 11 clinics across 7 states (Alabama, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania). This subject population was chosen because such individuals are known to use not only opiates and opioids but also a wide range of additional types of drugs at various levels ( ; ; ). An additional advantage of studying these applicants is that they have no reason to falsify (i.e., adulterate or substitute) the urine specimen requested at clinic intake, because it is needed to establish their eligibility for treatment. In spite of this, we still checked urine creatinine and pH levels (see below). The clinics provided a convenience sample of participants based on the clinics’ interest and ability to participate in this research. Applicants were eligible for the study if they were between 18–70 years old, not applying to a methadone program directly from a residential treatment, institutional or incarceration setting; and not transferring from another methadone program, although this last criterion was relaxed towards the end of the data collection when it became clear that methadone transfers were also usually misusing drugs. Oral fluid and urine specimens needed to be collected on the first day of intake, but eventual admission to the program was not required. The data were collected between Sept. 2020 and Nov. 2022. The participants were 46.4% male, 43.2% female and 10.4% other/no answer; 69.7% White, 7.2% African American, 4.0% Latino/a, 3.4% Native American and 15.7% other/no answer. 2.2 Training and Approval All oral fluid and urine specimens and other data were collected by clinic intake counselors and nurses. The clinic staff completed human subjects protection Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI) remote trainings. Remote trainings in study procedures were conducted for each clinic by study staff. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Western Michigan University. 2.3 Study Procedures. Applicants for methadone treatment were invited to participate in the study as part of their clinic intake process. Participation was voluntary and based on verbal consent because the data collection was anonymous; no subject identifying data were collected by the study and no individually identifiable study data were shared with the clinics. Data were linked by a research number. The objective was to collect the urine and oral fluid specimens for the study within 30 minutes of each other, although data were retained if the time interval was longer (see below). Urines for the study were obtained by pipetting 5ml from the clinic’s intake urine into a separate vial. Urines were unobserved per the clinics’ standard practice. Oral fluid specimens were obtained using the Quantisal collection device ( ). Oral fluid collection required at least 10 minutes to pass after any eating or drinking by the subject before giving the specimen. The specimens were mailed overnight to Forensic Fluids Laboratories where they were frozen at −20 deg C until weekly analysis. The participants were compensated with $20 gift cards good for food (not alcohol or tobacco) at a local supermarket chain. 2.4 Toxicological analysis Oral fluid was analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and urine by homogeneous enzyme immunoassay (HEIA), the latter being a liquid reagent immunoassay which is the industry standard for urine.

The specimens were mailed overnight to Forensic Fluids Laboratories where they were frozen at −20 deg C until weekly analysis. The participants were compensated with $20 gift cards good for food (not alcohol or tobacco) at a local supermarket chain. 2.4 Toxicological analysis Oral fluid was analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and urine by homogeneous enzyme immunoassay (HEIA), the latter being a liquid reagent immunoassay which is the industry standard for urine. HEIA was not used for oral fluid because the detection limits at the time that this study was planned were not low enough to detect low concentrations of drugs in oral fluid. Both oral fluid and urine were analyzed by LC–MS-MS whether or not the screening tests were positive. Standard commercial ELISA and HEIA kits and cutoffs used are shown in . shows the linear ranges for the LC-MS-MS analyses for urine and oral fluid. The limits of quantification (LOQ) cutoffs are the low values of the ranges. We decided to use urine cutoffs at the levels recommended by the federal government ( ), since even many non-regulated employers use these guidelines ( ), although we recognize lower cutoffs are also often used both clinically and for research (e.g., ). The exceptions were morphine and codeine, where we used cutoffs less than the recommended 2000 ng/mL because we needed to measure lower concentrations for research purposes. Cutoffs for oral fluid were determined by limit of quantification (LOQ) analysis with internal standards during method validation conducted by Forensic Fluids Laboratories. For purposes of this paper, we also classified an oral fluid or urine LC-MS-MS result as positive if there was a signal for a drug (“present”) even though it could not be quantified; this avoids underestimating the prevalence of a drug when presenting qualitative results. 2.5 Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics are presented for the various drugs and drug classes tested by IA and LC-MS-MS in oral fluid and urine. Associations between test results in paired specimens are determined by cross-tabulations. The complete tabulations are not always explicitly shown, although their statistical significance as computed by the McNemar test may be. The McNemar test for asymmetry in paired data measures the degree of imbalance based on the two discordant cells in any 2 × 2 crosstabulation of test results, each classified as positive (+) or negative (−) ( ). For example, is oral positive/urine negative more or less likely than oral negative/urine positive, or are these two combinations equally likely? If not equally likely based on statistical significance of p < .05, then the prevalences of the given drug or drug class are unequal on the tests. The minimal sample size required for the McNemar test is at least ten discordant pairs, assuming Yates correction. Cohen’s kappa (k) is a summary measure of agreement between the results of test #1 and test #2, each classified as positive vs. negative, with k = 0 indicating agreement expected by chance alone (based on the marginal distributions) and k = 1 indicating perfect agreement ( ). Values between 0 and 1 indicate increasing agreement beyond chance (although less than .60 is characterized as “weak” agreement) and values less than 0, which are rare in actual research, indicate less agreement than expected by chance alone. All statistical analyses were conducted with SPSS version 27. 2.6. Specimen validity parameters Creatinine was measured in all urine specimens. 22 participants tested < 20 ng/mL which is possibly indicative of dilution ( ), but in addition to participants having no incentive to do this, all those with low creatinine also tested positive for multiple drugs in urine; thus all those with ostensibly low creatine levels were retained in the analysis. No participants tested >300 ng/ml creatinine, which would be indicative of an adulterated specimen. The number of participants with paired oral fluid and urine specimens was 1099, of whom the time interval between the urine and oral fluid specimens could be calculated for 1076. This time interval was <30 minutes for 97.9% of the sample. Of the remaining, one extreme outlier subject (545 minutes) was excluded. Analyses were then conducted to determine whether there were any associations between time interval (classified as <30 minutes vs. >30 minutes) and disagreement on screening test results (classed as positive vs. negative) for major drug categories: opiates, cocaine, amphetamine-type stimulants and benzodiazepines; there were no statistically significant differences (p > .05). In addition, all urine pH values were in the acceptable range (> 3 and < 11) according to the vendor. 3. Results 3.1. The unconfirmed results are for the record only, because IA plus confirmation of positives is the standard clinical protocol. The initial IA test results for amphetamines and methamphetamines were combined into one category, “amphetamine-type stimulants,” because amphetamines, while subject to misuse directly, are also the main metabolites of methamphetamines, and the correlation between test results for amphetamines and methamphetamines is very high. A participant was classified as positive for amphetamine-type stimulants if they were positive on either the amphetamine or methamphetamine immunoassays. Statistical comparisons could not be made for ketamine and synthetic cannabinoids because of insufficient positives; this results in subsequent analyses for ten drug classes. As expected, shows that confirmed IA prevalences are the same or less than unconfirmed for both oral fluid and urine due to the elimination of false IA positives. Confirmed IA prevalences for urine are significantly higher than for oral fluid for 7 out of the 10 drug classes where comparisons can be made - benzodiazepines, cannabis, cocaine, methadone, opiates, oxycodone and tramadol (p < .05, McNemar’s test), whereas prevalence by oral fluid is never higher for any class. The third and sixth columns in show the prevalences of the drug classes as measured by LC-MS-MS for oral fluid and urine, respectively. That is, a positive result for a drug class was indicated if any specific drug belonging to that class was found to be positive by LC-MS-MS. As expected, prevalences by LC-MS-MS were either the same or higher than prevalences by confirmed IA for both oral fluid and urine due to the elimination of false IA negatives. Prevalences by LC-MS-MS were significantly higher for urine than oral fluid for two drug classes, cocaine and methadone, and significantly higher for oral fluid than urine for two drug classes, buprenorphine and tramadol. Columns one and two in show the magnitudes of the increases in drug class prevalences as measured by LC-MS-MS vs. confirmed IA for oral fluid and urine, respectively. Magnitude is defined as the ratio of LC-MS-MS prevalence to confirmed IA prevalence. This ratio averaged over 10 drug classes is 1.40 for oral fluid and 1.05 for urine. For oral fluid, column one in shows that the largest differences in drug prevalences between LC-MS-MS and confirmed IA are for tramadol, benzodiazepines, and oxycodone. For urine, column two in shows the largest differences are for methadone, benzodiazepines oxycodone, although the differences are very small. Column three in quantifies the differences in drug class prevalences by LC-MS-MS between oral fluid and urine that are seen in . For example, cocaine is 1.39 times as likely to be found in urine than in oral fluid, whereas buprenorphine was 0.7 times as likely to be found in urine than in oral fluid. There is no overall significant difference in drug use prevalence between oral fluid and urine when averaged over all 10 possible drug classes. 3.2. Discussion Within a confirmed IA testing protocol, urine appears to have some advantage over oral fluid in sensitivity for detecting most of the major drug classes, because most of the screens focus on metabolites of the active drugs, the former being more persistent in urine, with the caveat that this presumes universal validity of the oral fluid and urine specimens. The present study meets this condition, and oral fluid collection can always be observed, but of course the validity of urine specimens is often problematic in routine clinical and laboratory donation settings. Perhaps the latter is reason enough to prefer oral fluid testing in many settings, especially since the differences in accuracy of oral fluid vs. urine testing as measured by differences in drug prevalences are usually not large and can be mitigated to a considerable extent by conducting multiple tests. This deserves some elaboration. The results of the present study as well as most previous studies with paired oral fluid/urine specimens are based on a single test (donation) per subject, a situation unlikely to occur clinically, where multiple tests over a relatively short period are either available or could be obtained, e.g., in methadone treatment clinics or chronic pain clinics. (In fact, there are cautions about making major clinical decisions based on a single toxicology.) While a patient would be less likely to be positive on any single less sensitive test, several such tests within a defined time period would likely identify as many persons with substance use disorders as a single more sensitive test. This is true theoretically and could be verified empirically by the data collected by at least two previous studies. These are , who have oral fluid and urine test data from 5,061 paired tests conducted for 2,746 unique patients and , who have 1,544 paired tests conducted for 133 unique patients; however, such analysis was not performed. Note that multiple oral fluid testing is especially feasible (though there might be increased cost), which could compensate for its lower sensitivity as compared with urine testing for certain classes of drugs. Thus, differences in sensitivity between oral fluid and urine testing of the magnitudes observed for most drug classes in this study should not unduly influence the choice of test matrix for clinical monitoring purposes. This suggestion holds for both confirmed IA and direct-to-definitive testing protocols. We will now discuss differences between oral fluid and urine in direct-to-definitive LC-MS-MS results as shown in . Although there is no difference in detection of amphetamine-type stimulants as a class, amphetamines specifically are more detectable in urine than oral fluid. This may be because amphetamines, in addition to being ingested directly, are also the main metabolites of methamphetamine, and urine tends to be superior for detecting persistent metabolites. Methamphetamine (“crystal meth”) is a frequently misused drug equally prevalent in oral fluid and urine. The study also tested for several other drugs among amphetamine-type stimulants – MDEA, MDMA, phentermine – but found only one positive. MDMA (Ecstasy, Molly) particularly has been prominent on the electronic music club scene among young people ( ), but apparently has not penetrated into the population of this study. In the benzodiazepine category, a large majority of the positives by LC-MS-MS are attributable to alprazolam (Xanax) and oxazepam (Serax). However, oral fluid appears almost entirely insensitive to oxazepam, whereas it is more sensitive than urine to alprazolam. Previous research has reported that urine is generally more sensitive to detection of benzodiazepines than oral fluid ( ; ), but our finding is that the preferred matrix seems to depend on the particular benzodiazepine. Buprenorphine as a category was more frequently detected in oral fluid, although only the parent buprenorphine was found significantly more frequently in oral fluid; agreement beyond chance between oral fluid and urine was low (kappa = .52). This differs from the findings by and where buprenorphine was more prevalent in urine. In particular, found 90.5% positive for the buprenorphine parent by urine and 78.9% by oral fluid. However, this previous research employed higher cutoffs for oral fluid and lower cutoffs for urine, which could easily account for difference with the current study. For instance, 60% of the buprenorphine parent positives in the current study showed concentrations below the 1.0 ng/mL cutoff employed by . If had been able to employ a lower cutoff of 0.1 ng/mL as in our study, the difference between the matrices might well have been eliminated. A similar conclusion could be reached with respect to

This also points out the potentially important role of cutoffs in interpreting the findings of different studies relating to matrix differences; studies with varied findings should not necessarily be interpreted as either “right” or “wrong.” Although agreement on cannabis detection was only moderate (kappa = .65), there was no significant difference in prevalence between oral fluid and urine. Using the same measures, found higher prevalence of cannabis in urine, but that study’s higher cutoff for delta-9 THC (2.0 ng/mL) for oral fluid may explain the difference in findings. At our study’s cutoff of 0.1 ng/mL, 42% of the positives were between 0.1 – 2.0 ng/mL. Thus, if had been able to employ our cutoff, it is likely considerably more positives would have been obtained for oral fluid in their study. Cocaine as a category was more likely to be detected in urine, which was attributable to the greater likelihood of finding benzoylecgonine (BZE) in urine, the major metabolite of cocaine, due its now well-known longer elimination time in urine (Huestis, 2009). There was no significant difference in detecting the parent drug, cocaine. Research has been inconsistent about whether oral fluid or urine is the preferred matrix for detecting cocaine use ( ; ; ; ). found higher prevalence of cocaine/BZE in oral fluid than in urine, but the parent cocaine was only measured in oral fluid. The present study, which includes the largest number of cocaine/BZE positives in the relevant literature other than , shows that for unselected persons with substance use disorders, urine is at least slightly more sensitive than oral fluid to cocaine use, due to the wider window of detection of BZE in urine. This may have been assumed previously, but until now had not been statistically demonstrated. Overall, fentanyl as a category was equally prevalent in oral fluid and urine, although the parent fentanyl had higher prevalence in oral fluid and the major metabolite norfentanyl had higher prevalence in urine. In comparison, , based on a smaller number of positives, found fentanyl (defined as detection of the parent or metabolite) to be more prevalent in oral fluid (2.9%) vs. urine (2.0%), although this small difference might no longer be statistically significant if adjustment were made for autocorrelation, i.e., multiple test runs on the same individuals. More recently, again for a smaller sample of paired specimens, fentanyl was detected more often in urine (19.0%) than oral fluid (14.8 %), but “fentanyl” was defined differently for the two matrices – the urine test included norfentanyl but the oral fluid test did not, which clearly affects the matrix comparison ( ). Our fentanyl results are based on a large number of fentanyl positives due to the emergence of the national fentanyl epidemic during the period of data collection. Because our sampling recruited individuals with opioid use disorder, it would be expected that they would be prime consumers of fentanyl now that it has become readily available as a street drug ( ). Our findings have important implications for tracking the fentanyl epidemic in real-time epidemiological research using oral fluid as a highly feasible method of specimen collection. Ketamine was not a prominent street drug at the time of the study, although its therapeutic applications seem to be increasing recently, which through diversion might make it more available as a street drug in the future (e.g., ). Both the parent drug methadone and especially its main metabolite 2-ethylene-1,5-dimethyl-3,3-diphenylpyrrolidine (EDDP) were more likely to be detected in urine. This is based on by far the largest number of methadone positives for oral fluid and urine reported in the literature to date. The concentrations found in our study were consistent with those previously reported for individuals receiving methadone maintenance treatment ( ). The higher prevalence of EDDP in urine is most likely due to its long excretion time. Nonetheless, for the purpose of monitoring therapeutic ingestion of methadone, there would be little difference based on combined results for both the parent methadone and EDDP – 34% positive for urine and 29% for oral fluid. The higher prevalence of EDDP in urine is most likely due to its long excretion time. Nonetheless, for the purpose of monitoring therapeutic ingestion of methadone, there would be little difference based on combined results for both the parent methadone and EDDP – 34% positive for urine and 29% for oral fluid. As for the relatively high prevalence of methadone, this is likely due to participants transferring to several of the study clinics from other methadone programs and to use of “street” methadone ( ; ). However, they almost always also tested positive for a variety of other drugs. Opiates as a class were equally likely to be detected in oral fluid and urine, but there was variation between oral fluid and urine depending on the specific opiate. Oral fluid was considerably more sensitive to the presence of 6-monoacetylmorphine (6-MAM), a unique metabolite of heroin ( ), which is a consistent previous finding ( ; ; ; ). Oral fluid was also more sensitive to the presence of codeine (similar to ) and hydrocodone (Vicodin). When the parent hydrocodone and its metabolite norhydrocodone are combined as indicators of hydrocodone ingestion, hydrocodone remains significantly more prevalent in oral fluid. Urine appears to be more sensitive to hydromorphone (Dilaudid) and there was no difference between the matrices on morphine, which is a major metabolite of many opiates, and likely accounts for the overall finding of no difference between the matrices on the prevalence of opiates. Previous research has been inconsistent on this, with reporting morphine more prevalent in urine but in oral fluid. report results similar to ours for hydromorphone and morphine. Oxycodone as a category was equally likely to be present in oral fluid and urine, although there was a non-significant tendency for the oxycodone parent to be found more often in oral fluid and the metabolite oxymorphone more often in urine, which is consistent with the report by for a larger sample of oxycodone and oxymorphone positives. Note that oxymorphone (Opana) may also be detected as the primary drug ingested, although the extended release version was withdrawn from the market in 2017. Tramadol was more likely to be detected in oral fluid than urine, which is consistent with . Overall, our results regarding relative prevalence rates, based on a large sample, indicate oral fluid and urine are about equally efficient for monitoring overall opiate and opioid (synthetic opiate) use, unless there is a specific drug of therapeutic, research or epidemiological interest that needs to be targeted. This is most pertinent for heroin, where oral fluid is substantially superior to urine for the detection of one of its unique metabolites, 6-MAM. The two studies with the largest samples of paired oral fluid/urine specimens in the literature – the current study and - yielded generally consistent findings for direct-to-definitive testing for a wide range of drugs. Certain significant differences, e.g., for buprenorphine and cannabis, can apparently be explained by differences in cutoff levels. 4.1. Study Limitations The findings are for the specified laboratory-based IA tests; this could vary if different IA tests including point of care (POC) tests with different sensitivities and specificities were to be used. The potential benefit of direct-to-definitive testing in identifying specific drugs for which there are no generally used or practical IA screens was not addressed by this paper, but should be considered when making a decision about implementing direct-to-definitive testing in a clinical setting or for epidemiological purposes. The clinical implications of the study are limited by the design of a single test run per participant, as explained above. Not all drug classes of interest are well-represented, e.g., synthetic cannabinoids, due to rarity of use in the study’s participant population. The greater expense of direct-to-definitive as compared with presumptive with confirmation testing and its implications for clinical use were not examined by the study, although the difference in expense seems to be narrowing ( ). The study did not report drug concentrations in oral fluid and urine, which will be presented as a separate topic in a subsequent paper. However, in a few instances reference to concentrations was made to help in interpreting the qualitative test results. As in most previous similar studies, LC-MS-MS positives were determined by the limits of the technology; the study was not designed to investigate optimal cutoffs for clinical purposes. Finally, there is evidence that provider education is essential to properly interpret direct to definitive drug test results ( ; ) 5. Conclusions Urine analysis showed some technical advantage over oral fluid in sensitivity to several classes of drugs within a confirmed IA testing protocol, but this may be outweighed if there is reason to believe that tampering with urine

As in most previous similar studies, LC-MS-MS positives were determined by the limits of the technology; the study was not designed to investigate optimal cutoffs for clinical purposes. Finally, there is evidence that provider education is essential to properly interpret direct to definitive drug test results ( ; ) 5. Conclusions Urine analysis showed some technical advantage over oral fluid in sensitivity to several classes of drugs within a confirmed IA testing protocol, but this may be outweighed if there is reason to believe that tampering with urine specimens is a significant problem. Direct to definitive testing by LC-MS-MS yielded significantly higher prevalences for most drug classes than did confirmed IA, although the differences were more pronounced for oral fluid than urine. Direct-to-definitive testing yielded higher prevalences by urine for two and higher prevalences by oral fluid for two, out of 10 drug classes. However, oral fluid has a significant advantage specifically in detection of heroin use. In both confirmed IA and direct-to-definitive testing protocols, multiple oral fluid tests that are feasible in many clinical settings could compensate for the slightly lower sensitivity of oral fluid for certain drug classes. This study, based on one of the largest paired samples of oral fluid and urine specimens, with no incentive or reason for participants to tamper with their urine specimens, provides new information to assist treatment administrators, clinicians and researchers to decide on the optimal drug testing protocol for their specific environments.

chunks.content: Introduction People who inject drugs (PWID) have a high number of co-occurring medical conditions. In a large retrospective review of patients with active substance use, found hypertension (47%), tobacco use (46%), depression (43%), hyperlipidemia (24%), hepatitis C (HCV) (22%), and diabetes mellitus (21%) were among the most frequently recorded comorbid conditions. In a random sample of individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD), 91% had at least one documented chronic illness, with a mean of 2.6 chronic illnesses, and among individuals receiving methadone, 68% were prescribed at least one additional medication for the management of their chronic illness ( ). Further, one longitudinal cohort study of PWID identified that individuals with a detectable HIV viral load were more likely to have uncontrolled comorbid diseases like diabetes or hypertension ( ). Multimorbid diseases in this population are largely undiagnosed or undertreated ( ; ). Government organizations and national interest groups concerned with the health and wellness of PWID often limit the scope of their guidelines to harm reduction and infectious disease treatment and prevention. For example, guidelines from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for primary and preventative care of PWID focuses on infectious diseases, namely HIV, HCV, hepatitis B (HBV), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and tuberculosis (TB); these guidelines only mention the importance of referral and engagement in primary care for integrated services ( ). Recommendations for engaging individuals with substance use disorders in primary care for treatment of comorbid conditions are lacking, and often focus mostly on the delivery of safer use supplies via syringe access programs embedded within these sites ( ). The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) has offered funding to health care organizations that integrate mental health and primary care but with little attention paid to PWID ( ). An increasing number of providers are prepared to treat opioid use disorder (OUD) with evidence-based medications in the primary care setting. The 2016 Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA) allowed nurse practitioners and physicians associates to prescribe buprenorphine and expanded the accessibility and availability of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD). In addition, as x-waiver requirements continue to loosen and clinicians are able to treat limited numbers of patients with buprenorphine without completing onerous training, primary care providers can play a larger role in managing the holistic care of individuals with OUD ( ). Moving OUD treatment out of specialized substance use disorder treatment centers and into primary care is important as the healthcare needs of this population extend beyond treatment with MOUD and sequela related to injection drug use ( ). Existing literature has highlighted the multitude of reasons why people who use drugs, especially PWID, avoid healthcare environments. These reasons include previous negative experiences with stigmatizing healthcare providers and receipt of low-quality care that failed to address their needs ( ; ; ). Addressing these and other barriers to healthcare engagement and providing quality primary care to people who inject drugs is vital to improving chronic illness management in this population. In addition, providing positive and affirming healthcare experiences can counter the numerous documented and undocumented negative experiences that have historically pushed people who use drugs away from healthcare environments. Clinicians aiming to treat PWID in primary care settings may benefit from frameworks identifying barriers and facilitators to care engagement among marginalized populations. The Behavioral Model for Vulnerable populations, adapted from the Andersen Model for Healthcare Utilization, examines Predisposing, Enabling, Need, and Health Behavior characteristics associated with healthcare utilization and engagement ( ; ; ). Predisposing factors are individual characteristics and include age, race, gender, education, relationship status, and sexual orientation. Enabling characteristics are organizational and financial factors including health insurance status, health service resources, and region of residence. Need characteristics refer to those that are both perceived by an individual and those evaluated by healthcare providers. Finally, health behaviors are actions taken by PWID that inhibit or enable their ability to engage in their healthcare. This framework is useful to characterize the factors associated with healthcare utilization and engagement for this marginalized population. The purpose of this review, guided by the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, is to identify the barriers and facilitators to primary care engagement for PWID. Our review addresses a gap in knowledge regarding factors associated with primary care engagement among individuals with active injection drug use. Findings can be used to inform clinical interventions and future research to improve healthcare engagement among this population. Methods Search Strategy This review utilized the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) checklist for its organization and reported elements ( ). We searched PubMed, CINAHL, and EMBASE using a combination of MeSH (or CINAHL/EMBASE equivalent) for articles published between 2000–2020. Keywords searches combined common terms for 1) engagement in care (patient participation, patient acceptance of healthcare, patient compliance, utilization), 2) intravenous substance use, and 3) primary healthcare (primary, preventative health, primary prevention, secondary prevention, tertiary prevention). A comprehensive search strategy is listed in . We also reviewed reference lists from studies in the full test phase for additional studies that met inclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria The outcome of interest was engagement in primary care. Articles that reported a study population of people who actively inject drugs (within the past 12 months) and outcomes related to engagement in primary care were included. We define “engagement” broadly to encompass a wide range of outcomes. Previous literature has highlighted that people who use drugs may avoid healthcare environments due to past negative experiences. Thus, any level of engagement, even just receipt of medication, represents an opportunity to provide a positive healthcare experience and potentially change an individual’s perception of the benefits of engaging with healthcare providers. We characterized indicators for engagement in healthcare by any of the following outcomes: 1) Visits with a healthcare provider for disease diagnosis or management, including reported patient-provider relationship; 2) Receipt of or adherence to medications or health services, for example receipt and adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV; 3) Control of diagnosed disease, such as blood pressure control or curative treatment for Hepatitis C. Articles with study populations only partially made up of active PWID were considered for inclusion if they stratified analysis to include effect estimates for people who actively inject. We excluded studies focused on people reporting a history of injection drug use (but no current injection drug use), and those that did not explicitly measure injection drug use. Studies were also excluded if they did not explicitly measure engagement outcomes with PWID or did not report any domains related to engagement in primary care. Review articles, conference abstracts and qualitative studies were excluded. Articles without full-text unavailability or that were published in a language other than English were also excluded. Finally, given differences in healthcare delivery systems, study populations outside the United States were excluded. Data extraction Guided by the theoretical domains of the Behavior Model of Healthcare Utilization, we categorized studies by factors associated with the predisposing, enabling, need, or health behavior domains; studies could include factors that are in multiple domains of the framework. ‘Predisposing characteristics’ are existing characteristics that are not directly responsible for an individual’s decision to engage in care (ex. age, gender, race); ‘enabling conditions’ are facilitators or barriers to care engagement outside the individual’s control (ex. stigma, racism, structural barriers, delivery of salient services, etc.); ‘need conditions’ are divided into actual need (presence of a medical condition) and perceived need (the level to which patients desire care engagement); ‘health behaviors’ included substance use patterns and harm reduction uptake ( ; ; ). Two authors (OH and KT) conducted data extraction and quality assessments based on published guidelines ( ; ). With respect to the relationship with their PCP, PWID who reported a higher mean of harm reduction topics discussed with their PCP (p<0.001) and those whose PCP was aware of their substance use (p<0.001) were more likely to have a PCP visit in the last year ( ). Housing Both articles that examined the effect of housing found a deleterious effect of homelessness on engagement in care ( ; ). Among those living with HIV, those actively engaged in injection drug use were more likely to report homelessness compared to those who were not actively injecting (p<0.001); active PWID in that study were found to have worse health outcomes, even when utilizing HIV primary care ( ). Conversely, stable housing was significantly associated with uptake of ART (aOR 2.05; 95% CI 1.11–3.77) compared to PWID reporting unstable housing ( ). Peer norms One study demonstrated the positive influence of peers on engagement. Peers acted as social support during substance use disorder treatment and helped improve ART adherence and clinic appointment attendance ( ). Findings were limited to 14 patients in this feasibility study, but this peer support model demonstrated success in improving care engagement among PWID. Participants receiving peer support kept 84% of scheduled primary care appointments, and the intervention led to sustained ART adherence (90% of participants) and enrollment in substance use disorder treatment (75% of participants) ( ). Need factors associated with healthcare engagement Perceived need One study found that PWID with increased healthcare utilization (increased number of visits) had significantly increased odds of taking ART 6 months later (aOR 1.44; 95% CI 1.09–1.91) compared to PWID with less utilization ( ). Another study noted that rating HIV care as ‘very important’ (aOR 1.77; 1.31, 2.37) was significantly associated with having a HIV prevention discussion with a healthcare provider compared those who rated HIV care as less than ‘very important’ on a 4-point Likert scale ( ). Actual need In two studies, HIV disease stage was significantly associated with engagement in healthcare. PWID with a CD4 counts <350 were more likely than those with higher counts to be taking ART at the 6 month follow up visit (aOR 1.65; 95% CI 1.23–2.22), while those with CD4 counts >= 200 had more visits with a primary care provider than those with lower counts (aOR 1.64; 95% CI 1.10–2.46) ( ; ). Four studies measured diagnosed chronic health conditions among PWID. One study demonstrated that people actively injecting drugs were significantly more likely to be diagnosed with chronic infectious diseases (HIV, HCV, Hepatitis B) compared to past injection drug users (p<0.001) ( ). In another study, PWID living with HIV had 2 times higher adjusted odds of a major depression diagnosis compared to people living with HIV who did not report active injection drug use (95% CI 1.75–2.73) ( ). An additional study found that PWID with a higher reported mean of conditions treated by their PCP were more likely to have seen their PCP in the last year (p=0.04) ( ). While outcomes of engagement in care were measured differently, similarities included four studies which found negative associations with ART uptake and adherence ( ; ; ; ) while another four found decreased healthcare visits and satisfaction ( ; ; ; ) for participants who were actively injecting drugs. The remaining study found that PWID who injected daily in the last 6 months and PWID who injected at least once in the last 6 months were less likely to initiate and complete a Hepatitis B vaccine series compared to those who reported non-injection substance use ( ). Syringe exchange services One study measured the association between participation in harm reduction services and healthcare engagement. In their multivariable model, exchanging more needles per visit to a syringe exchange program was significantly associated with primary care utilization compared to those with a lower volume of needles exchanged (aOR 2.4; 95% CI 1.5–4.1) ( ). Discussion This systematic review identified factors related to engagement in primary care among people actively injecting drugs. Among the 23 included articles, the majority were observational studies utilizing descriptive designs. Although the assessment of evidence was primarily rated ‘good’, this review identifies a significant need to improve our understanding of primary care engagement for PWID. Two prior systematic reviews have been conducted with similar populations. conducted a systematic review that used the Andersen Healthcare Utilization Model to assess utilization of hospital-based outpatient services among people living with HIV. However, this review did not specifically focus on PWID. Another review conducted using literature published between 2000–2010 examined models of primary care delivery and the acceptability of these services by PWID ( ), but had an international focus and also did not restrict to active injection drug use. Additionally, , published an article related to primary care engagement among PWID, but did not take a systematic approach and only reported clinical care recommendations. Guided by the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, we synthesized factors within the model’s four domains, and their impact on engagement in primary care outcomes ( ). From the Enabling domain, patient-provider relationship emerged as a strong factor related to care engagement: across all the studies reviewed, positive patient-provider relationship was associated with greater engagement and negative relationships associated with less engagement. These findings were consistent with the broader literature of chronic disease management showing positive patient-provider relationships associated with higher levels of care engagement ( ; ). Co-location of services also emerged as a facilitator to primary care engagement, but studies associated with this finding were not highly rated due to limitations related to statistical analysis. Other international studies with PWID have also identified provision of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) in the primary care setting as a factor correlated to engagement in healthcare, though these international studies did not meet criteria for inclusion in this review ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Finally, current insurance status was associated with healthcare engagement across the five studies that measured it, but only two were published on data collected after the Affordable Care Act. These finding suggest that linkage to healthcare insurance could be more salient to healthcare engagement with the expansion of health insurance. One recent study found that PWID in Medicaid expansion states were more likely to have insurance (aPR 2.3; 95% CI 2.0–2.6) and have a usual source of healthcare (aPR 1.5; 95% CI 1.3–1.9) ( ) than PWID in non-expansion states. This study was not included in our analysis due to the authors’ definition of PWID including individuals reporting non-injection opioid use. Predisposing factors were not well measured or well represented across the studies with a few exceptions. Only one study stratified analysis by sex or gender but did not conduct analyses or provide effect estimates of engagement in care ( ). As a whole, measures and comparisons of race and ethnicity were also inconsistent. While differences in race as a predisposing factor were reported, little can be drawn from them without reported effect estimates and improved study design. Andro- and ethnocentrism was evident since many studies had samples that were over 50% male and rarely had balance in racial and ethnic groups, which also limits conclusions regarding sex, gender, race and ethnicity. As a whole, measures and comparisons of race and ethnicity were also inconsistent. While differences in race as a predisposing factor were reported, little can be drawn from them without reported effect estimates and improved study design. Andro- and ethnocentrism was evident since many studies had samples that were over 50% male and rarely had balance in racial and ethnic groups, which also limits conclusions regarding sex, gender, race and ethnicity. Evidence from the need domain described the complicated nature of care engagement for PWID. Studies demonstrated high burden of multimorbidity, difficulty engaging with accessible healthcare services that meet perceived needs, and the competing nature of active substance use with engagement in primary care. Health behaviors were most consistently measured across studies, with strong evidence that active injecting was a salient barrier to care engagement. This could be an area where clinicians can better assess injecting practices and provide harm reduction services in the primary care setting ( ) or co-locate health services within harm reduction centers ( ). There were limitations to this study. Filters on publishing date were applied to this systematic review, though we reviewed evidence over a 20-year period. This introduces bias as secular changes in healthcare policy and service access contribute greatly to healthcare engagement. Additionally, engagement in healthcare as an outcome proved difficult for data synthesis, as outcomes for engagement are wider ranging than healthcare utilization measures alone. This broader definition, however, allows for more nuanced analysis and understanding of healthcare needs of this population. Finally, many studies were excluded because they did not explicitly measure active injection drug use or stratify their results based on active injecting. Future studies with PWID would benefit from collecting and reporting on active versus historical injection drug use and incorporating a clear conceptual framework to define healthcare engagement outcomes. Clinical Relevance Nursing plays an important role in healthcare engagement for PWID. Recent evidence has shown that nurse-led clinics and the expansion of medications for opioid use disorder address critical gaps in these essential services for PWID, particularly in rural areas ( ; ; ; ; ). Additionally, nurses and nurse case managers working in the primary care setting play a critical role in addressing holistic care needs of patients, including some barriers identified by this review, and can engage PWID in primary care long term ( ; ). Overall, nurses in the primary care setting play an important role in addressing barriers to care engagement, improving access to essential substance use and primary care services, and developing meaningful patient-nurse and patient-care team relationships. Conclusions Although the preponderance of evidence is mixed, we identified several factors as barriers or facilitators to engagement in primary care for PWID. Given the ongoing overdose crisis, we must develop evidence-based strategies to engage individuals in the primary care setting for needs extending beyond infectious disease prevention and management and treatment of substance use disorders ( ). Clinical practice and research should continue to consider patients and research participants’ aggregate needs rather than the sum of their disease parts. While most of the studies here focused on engagement in HIV and substance use disorder care within the primary care setting, our findings can direct future research focused on PWID’s engagement in primary care broadly. chunks.content: Introduction The emergence of high-potency synthetic opioids (HPSO), such as fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, has led to an overdose crisis in the US. Methadone and buprenorphine are the most effective medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD), reducing overdoses and opioid-related mortality by up to 50%. To reduce overdose deaths, timely initiation and retention of methadone and buprenorphine are critical. While the drug supply has changed, clinical guidelines about methadone and buprenorphine initiation were based on research when heroin and prescription opioids dominated the opioid supply. , Standard guidance about methadone initiation begins with 30 to 40 mg taken orally followed by up-titration every 3 to 5 days. Guidance for the initiation of the partial opioid agonist buprenorphine begins with repeated doses of 2 to 4 mg; this begins only after opioid withdrawal symptoms emerge to decrease the risk of precipitated opioid withdrawal, an abrupt worsening of withdrawal symptoms due to buprenorphine displacing full opioid agonists on the opioid receptors. However, evidence suggests HPSOs complicate methadone and buprenorphine initiation due to their high affinity at the μ-opioid receptor, prolonged clearance due to lipophilicity, and creation of high tolerance. , , , , For methadone initiation, the high tolerance induced by HPSOs means the standard methadone approach may inadequately treat withdrawal, reducing retention early in treatment. For buprenorphine initiation, HPSOs are thought to lead to more challenging initiations and risk for precipitated opioid withdrawal. , , , Initiation of methadone and buprenorphine in the hospital setting has proven benefits. , With the ability to closely monitor patients and adequately address symptoms and complications, hospital-based addiction consult services (ACS) are at the forefront of innovations seeking to overcome methadone and buprenorphine initiation barriers fueled by HPSOs. ACS have described rapid (ie, faster dose escalation compared with standard initiation) methadone initiation protocols, and have found them to be feasible and effective. , , , Hospital ACS adapted buprenorphine initiations through several novel approaches, namely, the use of higher initiation doses (high-dose initiation) and the use of initially low but gradually increasing buprenorphine doses while overlapping full opioid agonists (low-dose initiation). Evidence, including the data synthetized by ACS, led to the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) releasing an expert-based guidance document addressing the adaptation of buprenorphine initiations to HPSOs. Despite reports of novel methadone and buprenorphine initiation practices, there remains a dearth of evidence describing the practices that ACS are using. We examined academic ACS directors’ self-report of perceptions of HPSOs and hospital-based methadone and buprenorphine initiation practices nationally. Methods Study Setting and Data Sources This survey study was deemed exempt from full review by the Yale University institutional review board. Reporting follows the American Association for Public Opinion Research ( AAPOR ) reporting guideline. From October 2023 to April 2024, we surveyed ACS directors associated with addiction fellowships about their current practices for hospital-based methadone and buprenorphine initiation from the 50 US states; Washington, DC; and Puerto Rico. We used public databases , to identify Accreditation Council of Graduate Medical Education (ACGME)–accredited addiction medicine fellowships (96 fellowships) and addiction psychiatry fellowships (54 fellowships) and lists of fellowship directors from the American College of Academic Addiction Medicine and the American Academy of Addiction Psychiatry. We emailed program directors to identify the directors of the ACS associated with their fellowship program. Study Sample and Recruitment Potential respondents were directors of hospital-based ACS affiliated with ACGME-accredited addiction medicine and addiction psychiatry fellowship programs. We chose this group because it is geographically diverse and likely to lead in methadone and buprenorphine initiation practice and educating addiction specialists. If more than 1 ACS was associated with a program, each service was included that provided services at distinct sites. Eligible respondents received a unique link to a self-administered online survey. Codirectors were sent a joint email with a unique survey link that could only be completed once to ensure no single ACS was overrepresented. We sent potential respondents up to 3 reminders. Respondents received a $50 electronic gift card for participation. Informed consent was obtained electronically prior to the start of the survey. Survey Development The survey (eAppendix in ) was based on a prior study assessing practice variation in low-dose buprenorphine initiation, literature and recent ASAM Clinical Consensus Statement, and the research team’s expert opinion. We examined the face validity of the survey through pilot testing with addiction medicine and addiction psychiatry clinicians. Case-based scenarios were refined using one-on-one cognitive interviews, a structured interview method used for eliciting understanding of the questions and thought process to ensure consistent interpretation. Cognitive interviews were conducted over video conference with a geographically diverse group of 3 addiction medicine and 3 addiction psychiatry specialists; after each interview, the cases were iteratively refined. Case-based scenarios were refined using one-on-one cognitive interviews, a structured interview method used for eliciting understanding of the questions and thought process to ensure consistent interpretation. Cognitive interviews were conducted over video conference with a geographically diverse group of 3 addiction medicine and 3 addiction psychiatry specialists; after each interview, the cases were iteratively refined. The survey included definitions for each methadone and buprenorphine initiation method. We defined standard methadone initiation based on 2021 Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration guidance as 40 mg maximum on day 1 with up-titration of 5 to 10 mg every 3 days. Rapid methadone initiation was defined as any initiation regimen more rapid than the standard initiation (using higher doses or shorter duration between dose escalations). We defined 3 buprenorphine initiation practices based on ASAM Clinical Considerations. (1) Traditional initiation starts with a first dose of 2 to 4 mg of buprenorphine after reaching moderate withdrawal. (2) High-dose initiation (ie, macrodosing) starts with the first dose (8-16 mg) of buprenorphine after reaching moderate withdrawal. (3) Low-dose initiation (ie, overlapping or microdosing) starts with low doses of buprenorphine (eg, 0.5 mg sublingual), which gradually increases while continuing full opioid agonists. We defined a fourth option, buprenorphine rescue (ie, buprenorphine administration after intentional naloxone-precipitated withdrawal) based on recent case reports. , Survey Variables Study data were collected and managed using REDCap. , We assessed perceived impact of the drug supply on methadone and buprenorphine initiation through a 5-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. We assessed if methadone and buprenorphine initiation were offered. If buprenorphine initiation was offered, we assessed use of long-acting injectable formulations prior to discharge. Regarding methadone initiation, we assessed the use of rapid initiation, additional use of full-agonist opioids to treat continued withdrawal, and other adjunctive medications to treat withdrawal (eg, clonidine). For services that used rapid methadone initiation, we assessed the proportion of initiations using rapid initiation in the last 2 weeks (1%-100% in 10% increments) as well as the clinical situations in which rapid initiation was used (ie, regular fentanyl use, pregnancy, prior premature discharge against medical advice, concomitant acute pain and OUD, recently discontinued methadone within last month, persistent withdrawal despite standard protocol, or other). We asked about the typical dose of methadone on days 1 to 5 of a rapid initiation through free-text response. For services that did not initiate methadone, we queried their approach to management of methadone prescribed as an outpatient. Regarding buprenorphine initiation, we used multiple choice questions assessing use of each of the buprenorphine initiation practices defined previously and the proportion of initiations using each practice in the last 2 weeks (1%-100% in 10% increments). Low-dose initiation was further characterized by the formulations of buprenorphine used (split films or tabs, buccal, transdermal, intravenous, and other) and the length of a typical low-dose initiation. We assessed typical selection of buprenorphine initiations practices using 7 case-based scenarios intended to represent common hospital scenarios. All cases pertained to hospitalized patients with severe OUD not interested in in other forms of MOUD. Discussion To our knowledge, this is the first survey study to systematically characterize hospital methadone and buprenorphine initiation practices for OUD in a national sample. Our study generated several key findings. First, we found widespread agreement that HPSOs had changed their practices of initiating methadone and buprenorphine. Second, of those that initiated methadone, most (81%) offered rapid methadone initiation with variable maximum daily doses. When opioid withdrawal symptoms continued during methadone initiation, nearly all services (96%) offered ancillary medications, with a majority (67%) utilizing full-agonist opioids. Third, all services initiated buprenorphine, most commonly with low-dose initiation, followed closely by traditional and high-dose initiation. Across 7 clinical scenarios, low-dose buprenorphine initiation remained the most frequently offered practice except in the scenario of a patient presenting in significant opioid withdrawal 2 days after last fentanyl use in which traditional or high-dose initiation were preferred. To our knowledge, this is the first study assessing hospital-based methadone initiation practices across different institutions. In the setting of higher opioid tolerances due to HPSOs and undertreated opioid withdrawal contributing to poor outcomes like premature hospital discharges, , adequate dosing of methadone and control of withdrawal is critical. Hospitalization is an opportunity to quickly achieve an effective methadone dose in a monitored setting to maximize the potential for improved treatment retention , , , and offers a setting to utilize short-acting opioids for withdrawal management. We found widespread and frequent use of rapid methadone initiations with short-acting opioids for continued withdrawal symptoms. Together, these results show that practice changes, in response to an evolving drug supply, have outpaced clinical guidelines and rigorous research in this area, and that research is needed to fully elucidate risks and benefits of each novel initiation practice. Despite this research gap, our results suggest collective consensus among ACS directors of the benefits of more assertive approaches in the hospital setting that outweigh concerns about the risks. The impact of HPSOs on buprenorphine initiation is an area of ongoing research. There is widespread perception that buprenorphine-precipitated opioid withdrawal is increasingly common and that this is an underlying factor of buprenorphine initiation adaptations, which this study confirmed, , , yet hospital- and emergency department–based observational data has found widely variable rates of buprenorphine-precipitated opioid withdrawal ranging from 1% , to more than 10%. , , Regardless of the true incidence, our study suggests that ACS are adopting novel buprenorphine initiation practices such as low-dose initiation. For hospitalized patients for whom full-agonist opioids can be administered, low-dose buprenorphine initiation offers several additional potential advantages: reducing need for opioid withdrawal, expanding clinical situations in which buprenorphine can be initiated to include those in which opioids must be continued (ie, for acute pain or for a person currently treated with methadone), and being the novel method with the most robust observational hospital-based data. , , , Despite its common use, the specifics of low-dose initiation regimens, such as length of regimen and buprenorphine formulation, remain highly variable. , , , , , Future research should examine the comparative effectiveness of the different low-dose initiation regimens. Some variability in initiation should be expected given that ACS individualize care to adapt to the local drug supply and patient preference, yet, the amount of variability may reflect inconsistent dissemination and implementation of new practices, variable clinician comfort with practices prior to incorporation into guidelines, contradictory hospital and pharmacy guidance, and lack of comparative effectiveness data. As the drug supply continues to shift, as evidenced by new adulterants such as xylazine, guidelines are often not able adapt or be implemented quickly enough due to a lack of established evidence base and the known time lag in implementation of guidelines. Learning about health care systems and community-participatory research and leveraging the experience of the community of people who use drugs and community-based clinicians to understand and adapt to changes in the drug supply, such as through the Delphi Method, offers potential avenues to respond more quickly. An additional finding was the lack of self-identified racial and ethnic diversity among ACS directors. Despite overdose rates rising more quickly in racially and ethnically minoritized populations, particularly among Black, Hispanic, and American Indian or Alaska Native people, , , only 5% of our sample self-identified as Black, 10% identified as Hispanic, and none identified as American Indian or Alaska Native; this highlights the need to develop and invest in strategies to diversify and retain a workforce that reflects the communities they serve. Limitations This study has limitations. First, our study was limited to academic addiction fellowship–associated ACS in predominantly urban settings, and results may not generalize to services in other settings. Second, the study captured self-report of current practice, which may differ from actual practice. Third, we surveyed about adaptation in methadone and buprenorphine initiation based on published practices and thus may not have captured unpublished practices. Fourth, although our definitions (ie, rapid methadone initiation and low-dose buprenorphine initiation) were based on the literature and were provided throughout the survey, respondents may use different definitions to describe their practice, which may not have been adequately captured. Conclusions In this survey study of hospital-based ACS directors, we found widespread agreement that HPSOs impact methadone and buprenorphine initiation and widespread use of novel initiation practices in response. Rapid methadone initiation and adjunctive use of full-agonist opioids to treat additional withdrawal were common. Low-dose initiation of buprenorphine was the most common buprenorphine initiation method used. Future research should assess the safety and effectiveness of these adaptations on patient outcomes and use community-partnered research to aid in implementation of new adaptations in response to a continuously shifting drug supply. Leveraging community expertise to generate time-sensitive guidance, such as through the Delphi Method, may serve as an important bridge to adapt clinical care more rapidly.

Background Psychological trauma disproportionately affects people with HIV (PWH) compared with the general population. – Trauma refers to the harmful physical, psychological, social, or spiritual effects from exposure to adverse events (e.g., car accident, domestic violence, racism). – Among PWH, these effects are associated with deleterious health outcomes, including accelerated immune system suppression and HIV disease progression, reduced medication and appointment adherence, and unsuppressed viremia. – , , – Associated psychiatric risks include substance use disorders, major depression, and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), with a PTSD prevalence rate up to 74% among trauma-exposed PWH. , Together, the synergistic effects of HIV and trauma constitute a syndemic , and pose major barriers to the United States (U.S.) Ending the HIV Epidemic (EHE) goals. Consequent to the HIV-trauma syndemic, HIV care providers are repeatedly exposed to trauma as an occupational hazard. – This increased trauma exposure among providers can negatively impact professional quality of life (PQoL); – by reducing compassion satisfaction and leading to vicarious trauma. – Over time, these exposures contribute to chronic exhaustion, reduced empathy, hypervigilance, minimization, a sense of persecution, guilt, anger/cynicism, addictions, and feelings of hopelessness. , At least two-thirds of HIV care providers nationally experience burnout, including depersonalization, apathy, and disengagement from patients. , These effects, in turn, are associated with reductions in patient satisfaction and provider trust, appointment non-adherence, and potential re-traumatization of PWH and their care providers. – Trauma-informed care (TIC) is an evidence-based approach for mitigating the effects of trauma throughout healthcare systems. , In TIC systems, personnel are trained and provided institutional resources with which to recognize and respond to trauma while resisting re-traumatization. Typically, the training and resources foster six general TIC principles: Safety; Trustworthiness and Transparency; Peer Support; Cross-Sector Collaboration and Mutuality; Empowerment, Voice, and Choice; and Cultural, Historical, and Gender Issues. , TIC interventions are associated with decreased trauma effects, increased resilience, and improved HIV outcomes among PWH. , – Knowledge gaps remain around TIC implementation. First, little is known about effective implementation strategies. Although community engagement approaches like Community-Based Participatory Research (CBPR) align with TIC principles (e.g., collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice, and choice), limited literature depicts CBPR as a TIC implementation strategy. Second, more concrete operationalization of the TIC principle Cultural, Historical, and Gender Issues is required to actionize this principle. Cultural Responsiveness might be an appropriate operationalization of this principle , – and refers to how providers approach consumers with an understanding that individuals from different backgrounds experience and respond to trauma differently, and these differences can impact behaviors and relationships. However, no studies have explored how cultural responsiveness explicitly relates to TIC. Finally, few studies document TIC implementation in Southern community-based HIV Organizations (CBOs) or across city-wide HIV care networks. To address these gaps, we applied a CBPR approach to conduct pre-implementation stage research to develop a data-driven plan for implementing TIC across a city-wide HIV care network in the Southern U.S. Methods Study Setting The Southern U.S. accounts for more than half of all new national HIV infections. In Nashville, Tennessee (TN), HIV rates are almost double that of the nation, and Black men who have sex with men (MSM) carry a disproportionate disease burden. A recent study shows PTSD rates are high (51%) among sampled PWH in the area. However, a local community-informed trauma intervention was associated with improvements in retention in medical care and viral suppression among trauma-affected PWH. Discussion A CBPR approach was applied to collaboratively conduct pre-implementation stage research to develop a community- and data-driven TIC implementation plan for a metro-wide HIV care network. Results from PM and key informant interviews indicate there are limited trauma assessments and services provided in the HIV care network, but there is tension for change and an implementation climate compatible with TIC. There was an observed need for scaling up trauma services, personnel trauma training and wellness initiatives, systematic efforts to integrate end-user preferences into services, diversify leadership championship, prioritize and foster cultural responsiveness, and coordinate city-wide efforts by leveraging resources. Our findings contribute to the TIHC knowledge base in several novel ways. To our knowledge, this is the first study to qualitatively explore implementation determinants of a city-wide trauma-informed HIV care network. However, the observed need for greater collaboration across the network is similar to previous TIC literature in other settings , and collectively underscore the importance of network-level and multi-disciplinarian implementation efforts. The recommendation to launch a city-wide coordinating center appears to be a novel strategy for leveraging resources to build a greater macro-level infrastructure for HIV care. We believe our cultural responsiveness findings also mark the first of its kind (i.e., in an HIV setting as part of TIC) and provide empirical support for diversifying TIC championship and broadening efforts to integrate humanistic communication. Finally, our efforts to include community members or end-users as co-producers of TIC implementation appear to be unique and provide methods for future investigators conducting trauma-informed research (i.e., research conducted through methods that actionize TIC principles). Though trauma was realized as pervasive and trauma services were a marked priority, trauma screening, referrals and services, and training were limited. There was a noted cost of maintaining the status quo (i.e., not implementing TIC) in which the network as a whole appears to insufficiently attend to mental health. While 83% of sampled Ryan White clinics in the Southeastern U.S. report providing mental health care on-site, 75% of HIV-focused CBOs in the Southern U.S. report insufficient community mental health services, and only 43% report having routine procedures for patient trauma screening. Our findings appear to be consistent with national, regional, and local findings, with the latter findings also indicating the need to improve the quality of mental health services in the catchment area. Moreover, consistent with TIC literature, , , , we observed significant interest in TIC adoption within a workforce who have received little TIC training. These results underscore the need for carrying out the summit recommendation to create a shared communication system to facilitate networking, referrals, and training. The noted need for greater staff wellness initiatives is also consistent with the TIC literature , and appears to be a modifiable component of PQoL. – While one-third of HIV care personnel report high levels of burnout, only one-third of CBOs address personnel vicarious trauma. This represents a critical omission given the trauma burden experienced by PWH, and the documented likelihood for vicarious trauma among HIV care personnel. While wellness campaigns excluding mental health have not improved clinical outcomes for staff, – those including mental health support have been associated with reductions in stress, anxiety, and depression and improvements in well-being. Further, several strategies for improving personnel mental health, have been found to be effective in various settings. Hence, improving personnel mental wellness was found to be important according to personnel in the HIV care network, a critical aspect of wellness campaigns generally, and an effort supported by empirical findings. The observed need for systematic efforts to engage community members or end-users as collaborative designers of services and policies is similar to that observed in other Southern CBO spaces.
